# REGIONAL ACROPORA PALMATA ANALYSIS

1.  This initial block establishes the analytical environment and prepares the dataset for subsequent modeling. It begins by clearing the workspace and loading the required libraries (`here`, `readxl`, `dplyr`, `ggplot2`, `stargazer`). The script then imports the updated regional chronology file (`ages_kernel_reg_updt.xlsx`) and filters the records to retain only *Acropora palmata* within the 0–6 ka interval. A custom function, `calc_density_summary()`, is defined to generate kernel density estimates through repeated resampling, thereby producing robust distributions of temporal signals. The function calculates quantiles (2.5%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 97.5%) and summarizes the median density across centennial intervals, including measures of variability and standard error. Finally, the procedure is applied to each site and to the aggregated regional dataset, yielding two consolidated objects: `signal_all`, which contains the simulated density curves, and `centennial_density_all`, which provides centennial summaries of temporal variability. This chunk thus establishes the foundation for reproducible density analyses across sites and at the regional scale.

```{r,echo=FALSE}
rm(list=ls(all=TRUE))
gc()
#install.packages("here")
library(here)
setwd(here::here())
library(readxl)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(stargazer)

datos_reg <- read_excel("ages_kernel_reg_updt.xlsx")

datos_reg_pal <- datos_reg %>%
  filter(group == "palmata", t_ka >= 0 & t_ka <= 6)

calc_density_summary <- function(df, spot_name){
  df$t_ka <- as.numeric(df$t_ka)
  
signalmx <- matrix(ncol = 512, nrow = 1000)
  for(i in 1:nrow(signalmx)){
    signalmx[i,] <- density(df$t_ka[sample(1:nrow(df), min(40, nrow(df)))],
                            bw = 0.09, from = 0, to = 6)$y
  }
  
  x <- seq(0, 5.999, length.out = 512)   
  
signal_df <- data.frame(
    x      = x,
    q025   = apply(signalmx, 2, quantile, 0.025),
    q975   = apply(signalmx, 2, quantile, 0.975),
    q25    = apply(signalmx, 2, quantile, 0.25),
    q75    = apply(signalmx, 2, quantile, 0.75),
    median = apply(signalmx, 2, median),
    spot   = spot_name
  )
  
 breaks <- seq(0, 6, by = 0.1)
  mids   <- breaks[-length(breaks)] + diff(breaks)/2
  
  centennial_summary <- signal_df %>%
    mutate(interval = cut(x, breaks = breaks, include.lowest = TRUE, right = TRUE)) %>%
    group_by(interval) %>%
    summarise(
      avg_median = mean(median, na.rm = TRUE),
      sd_median  = sd(median, na.rm = TRUE),
      n_obs      = n(),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    mutate(
      se_median    = sd_median / sqrt(n_obs),
      interval_mid = mids[as.numeric(interval)],
      spot         = spot_name
    )
  
  return(list(signal_df = signal_df, centennial_summary = centennial_summary))
}

spots <- unique(datos_reg_pal$spot)
results_list <- lapply(spots, function(sp){
  df_spot <- datos_reg_pal %>% filter(spot == sp)
  calc_density_summary(df_spot, sp)
})

results_list <- c(results_list, list(calc_density_summary(datos_reg_pal, "Regional (All spots)")))

signal_all <- bind_rows(lapply(results_list, function(x) x$signal_df))
centennial_density_all <- bind_rows(lapply(results_list, function(x) x$centennial_summary))
```

2.  This code block constructs centennial binning of fossil ages for both site‑specific and regional datasets. After defining the temporal breaks (0–6 ka at 0.1‑ka intervals), the script filters the records of *Acropora palmata* and assigns each observation to an interval bin. For site‑level data, the maximum value of each bin is recorded to facilitate centennial alignment. A parallel procedure is applied to the full dataset, designating all observations as **“Regional”** and similarly calculating bin maxima. The two outputs are then merged into a single object (`centennial_counts_all`), which consolidates site‑specific and regional counts by centennial interval. This chunk therefore establishes the discrete temporal framework required for subsequent aggregation and comparative analyses across sites and scales.

```{r,echo=FALSE}
library(dplyr)

breaks <- seq(0, 6, by = 0.1)

datos_reg_pal <- datos_reg %>%
  filter(group == "palmata", t_ka >= 0 & t_ka <= 6)

centennial_counts_sites <- datos_reg_pal %>%
  mutate(interval_bin = cut(
    t_ka,
    breaks = breaks,
    include.lowest = TRUE,
    right = TRUE
  )) %>%
  mutate(interval_max = breaks[match(interval_bin, levels(interval_bin)) + 1])

centennial_counts_regional <- datos_reg %>%
  filter(group == "palmata", t_ka >= 0 & t_ka <= 6) %>%
  mutate(interval_bin = cut(
    t_ka,
    breaks = breaks,
    include.lowest = TRUE,
    right = TRUE
  )) %>%
  mutate(
    spot = "Regional",
    interval_max = breaks[match(interval_bin, levels(interval_bin)) + 1]
  )

centennial_counts_all <- bind_rows(centennial_counts_sites, centennial_counts_regional)
```

## *1. Data Overview*

3.  In this section we establish the graphical representation of centennial fossil counts, providing a visual foundation for comparative analysis across sites and define the color palette for generating site‑specific bar plots of fossil counts by centennial interval. A custom set of colors is assigned to each locality to ensure consistent visual identity across figures. The dataset is then binned into 0.1‑ka intervals, and counts of *Acropora palmata* fossils are aggregated by site. The resulting table is structured to include both the bin maxima and a fixed ordering of sites for reproducibility. Using `ggplot2`, the script produces a stacked bar chart in which fossil counts per 100‑year interval are displayed along the temporal axis (0–6 ka BP). The figure corresponds to the **Figure 3a** within the main text (**Reconstruction of regional coral abundance and paleoclimate trends. a. Counts of *Acropora palmata* ages in 100-year intervals from reef sites are used as response variables for modelling)** and emphasizes site‑level differences in temporal distribution, with clear labeling, minimal gridlines, and a standardized legend.

```{r,echo=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

custom_colors <- c(
  "Punta Maroma" = "#D55E00",              
  "Regional (All spots)" = "#332288",
  "Regional"             = "#332288",
  "Saint Croix" = "#F0E442",         
  "Belize" = "#CCBB44",    
  "Florida" = "#0072B2"
)

breaks <- seq(0, 6, by = 0.1)

centennial_counts_sites <- datos_reg_pal %>%
  mutate(interval_bin = cut(t_ka, breaks = breaks, include.lowest = TRUE, right = TRUE)) %>%
  group_by(spot, interval_bin) %>%
  summarise(counts = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(interval_max = breaks[match(interval_bin, levels(interval_bin)) + 1],
         spot = factor(spot, levels = c("Belize", "Saint Croix", "Florida", "Punta Maroma")))


pr<-ggplot(centennial_counts_sites,
       aes(x = interval_max, y = counts, fill = spot)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "stack", alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = custom_colors) +
  labs(
    x = "Time (ka BP)",
    y = "Acropora palmata  \n fossils/100 years",
    fill = "Site"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(0, 6, 0.5),
    minor_breaks = seq(0, 6, 0.5)
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 6))
pr
ggsave("counts_plot.pdf", plot = pr, width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 300, device = cairo_pdf)
```

### *1.1 Acropora palmata* age densities (Site specific KDE)

4.  This code block integrates site‑level and regional density outputs into a structured comparative framework and produces both tabular and graphical summaries. After loading the necessary libraries and defining a consistent color palette, the script specifies temporal rectangles to highlight intervals of interest across sites. The `signal_all` and `centennial_density_all` objects are annotated with panel labels to distinguish local, zonal, and consolidated regional scales. Data are filtered to retain valid centennial intervals within the 0–6 ka range, and a summary table (`tabla_resumen`) is generated using the `gt` package to report mean densities, measures of dispersion, and extreme values by site. The graphical routine then overlays uncertainty ribbons, median density curves, and highlighted intervals on a unified plot, with customized legends and standardized axes. The figure represents the raw version of **Figure 2** from the main text (**Composite age-density plot of *Acropora palmata* abundance across Caribbean)** and is exported as a high‑resolution PDF, ensuring reproducibility and clarity for publication. This chunk thus consolidates the analytical outputs into interpretable visual and tabular formats, enabling direct comparison of temporal density patterns across spatial scales.

```{r,fig.width=12, fig.height=6,echo=FALSE}

library(dplyr)
library(knitr)
library(scales) 
library(colorspace)
library(ggplot2)
library(gt)

custom_colors <- c(
  "Punta Maroma" = "#D55E00",              
  "Regional (All spots)" = "#332288",
  "Regional"             = "#332288",
  "Saint Croix" = "#F0E442",         
  "Belize" = "#CCBB44",    
  "Florida" = "#0072B2"
)

rects<-data.frame(
  xmin = c(0.71, 1.99, 2.2,3.68,5.1,5.54),
  xmax = c(1.44, 2.72,3.0, 4.20,5.9,6.00),
  ymin = -Inf,
  ymax = Inf,
  spot = c("Punta Maroma", "Belize","Regional (All spots)","Belize", "Regional (All spots)","Belize"))
  
  
  
signal_all <- signal_all %>%
  mutate(panel = case_when(
    spot == "Punta Maroma" ~ "a) Local (Punta Maroma)",
    spot == "Florida" ~ "b) Local (Florida)",
    spot %in% c("Saint Croix","Belize") ~ "c) Regional (by zones)",
    spot == "Regional (All spots)" ~ "d) Consolidated Regional"
  ))


centennial_density_all <- centennial_density_all %>%
  mutate(panel = case_when(
    spot == "Punta Maroma" ~ "Punta Maroma",
    spot == "Florida" ~ "Florida",
    spot == "Belize" ~ "Belize",
    spot == "Saint Croix" ~ "Saint Croix",
    spot == "Regional (All spots)" ~ "Regional"
  ))

signal_all <- signal_all %>%
  filter(!is.na(panel)) %>%
  mutate(panel = droplevels(factor(panel)))

centennial_density_all <- centennial_density_all %>%
  filter(!is.na(panel)) %>%
  mutate(panel = droplevels(factor(panel)))
centennial_density_all <- centennial_density_all %>%
  filter(!is.na(interval_mid), interval_mid >= 0, interval_mid <= 6)


tabla_resumen <- centennial_density_all %>%
  group_by(panel) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_density = mean(avg_median, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_density   = mean(sd_median, na.rm = TRUE),
    se_density   = mean(se_median, na.rm = TRUE),
    min_density  = min(avg_median, na.rm = TRUE),
    min_interval = interval_mid[which.min(avg_median)],
    max_density  = max(avg_median, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_interval = interval_mid[which.max(avg_median)],
    n_intervals  = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(panel)

tabla_resumen %>%
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Summary of centenarian densities by site",
    subtitle = "average, dispersion, and extremes"
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(columns = c(mean_density, sd_density, se_density,
                         min_density, max_density,
                         min_interval, max_interval),
             decimals = 3)

custom_colors_plot <- custom_colors[names(custom_colors) %in% unique(signal_all$spot)]

p<-ggplot(signal_all, aes(x = x)) +
  geom_rect(data = rects,
    aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = 0.88, ymax = 0.98, fill = spot),
      inherit.aes = FALSE,
    alpha = 0.1) +
  geom_ribbon(data = subset(signal_all, spot == "Regional (All spots)"),
    aes(ymin = q025, ymax = q975, fill = spot), alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_ribbon(data = subset(signal_all, spot == "Regional (All spots)"),
    aes(ymin = q25, ymax = q75, fill = spot), alpha = 0.20) +
  geom_line(aes(y = median, color = spot), linewidth = 0.7) +
  scale_color_manual(values = custom_colors, guide = "legend") +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(
    "Punta Maroma" = 21,
    "Belize" = 22,
    "Florida" = 23,
    "Saint Croix" = 24,
    "Regional (All spots)" = 25
  ), guide = "legend") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = custom_colors, guide = "none") +
  guides(color = guide_legend("Region/Source",
                              override.aes = list(fill = custom_colors_plot)),
        shape = guide_legend("Region/Source")) +
  labs(x = "Time (ka BP)", y = "Density") +
  theme(strip.background = element_blank(),
        panel.background = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "bottom") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 6, 0.5),
                     minor_breaks = seq(0, 6, 0.5)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 6))
p
ggsave("Figure_2.pdf", plot = p, width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 300, device = cairo_pdf)
```

### 1.2 Densities' and fossil' counts Manipulation & Aggregation

5.  With this code block we initiate data manipulation adn data aggregation. Here we extract site‑specific and regional centennial density summaries using the previously defined function. The dataset is partitioned by locality (***Punta Maroma*****, *Florida*, *Belize*, *Saint Croix***) and each subset is processed through `calc_density_summary()` to generate centennial statistics of kernel density estimates. In addition, the full dataset is analyzed to produce a consolidated regional summary labeled “**Regional (All spots)**.” The outputs (`res_pm`, `res_fl`, `res_bz`, `res_sc`, `res_all`) contain centennial averages, dispersion measures, and interval midpoints for each spatial unit. This step ensures that both local and regional temporal signals are consistently quantified, providing the basis for comparative analyses across sites and scales.

```{r,echo=FALSE}
library(readxl)

df_pm <- datos_reg_pal %>% filter(spot == "Punta Maroma")
res_pm <- calc_density_summary(df_pm, "Punta Maroma")$centennial_summary

df_fl <- datos_reg_pal %>% filter(spot == "Florida")
res_fl <- calc_density_summary(df_fl, "Florida")$centennial_summary

df_bz <- datos_reg_pal %>% filter(spot == "Belize")
res_bz <- calc_density_summary(df_bz, "Belize")$centennial_summary

df_sc <- datos_reg_pal %>% filter(spot == "Saint Croix")
res_sc <- calc_density_summary(df_sc, "Saint Croix")$centennial_summary

res_all <- calc_density_summary(datos_reg_pal, "Regional (All spots)")$centennial_summary
```

6.  This code block summarizes the raw temporal distribution of fossil records across sites. Using the consolidated centennial dataset, the script groups observations by locality and calculates descriptive statistics for the age variable (*t_ka*). For each site, the output reports the number of records, mean and standard deviation of ages, minimum and maximum values, and the corresponding centennial intervals in which these extremes occur. The resulting table (`tabla_resumen_counts`) is formatted with the `gt` package to present a clear summary of sample size, central tendency, dispersion, and temporal range per site. This step provides a baseline characterization of the dataset, documenting the extent and variability of fossil ages before applying more complex density analyses.

```{r,echo=FALSE}
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
library(gt)
library(stringr)

tabla_resumen_counts <- centennial_counts_all %>%
  group_by(spot) %>%
  summarise(
    n_records   = n(),                               
    mean_t_ka   = mean(t_ka, na.rm = TRUE),         
    sd_t_ka     = sd(t_ka, na.rm = TRUE),           
    min_t_ka    = min(t_ka, na.rm = TRUE),          
    max_t_ka    = max(t_ka, na.rm = TRUE),          
    min_interval = interval_max[which.min(t_ka)],   
    max_interval = interval_max[which.max(t_ka)],   
    .groups = "drop"  ) %>%
  arrange(spot)


tabla_resumen_counts %>%
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Summary of fossil records by site (raw data)",
    subtitle = "Temporal distribution and dispersion per 0.1 ka bin"
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(mean_t_ka, sd_t_ka, min_t_ka, max_t_ka,
                min_interval, max_interval),
    decimals = 3
  )
```

### 1.3 Climatic Variables Manipulation & Aggregation

7.  This code block integrates climatic predictor data with the centennial fossil counts. The climate dataset (`df_GAM130326.xlsx`) is imported and converted to a data frame, after which temporal bins are defined at 0.1‑ka intervals. Each climatic record is assigned to its corresponding interval and the maximum boundary of the bin is calculated to ensure alignment with the fossil chronology. The centennial fossil counts (`centennial_counts_all`) are then merged with the climatic dataset by matching interval maxima, producing a unified table (`merged_df`). This merged dataset provides a consistent temporal framework in which fossil occurrence and climatic variables are directly comparable, thereby enabling subsequent statistical modeling of ecological responses to climate variability.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
datos_cli <- read_excel("df_GAM130326.xlsx")
datos_cli<-as.data.frame(datos_cli)

 
library(dplyr)

breaks <- seq(0, 6, by = 0.1)

datos_cli <- datos_cli %>%
  mutate(interval = factor(interval, levels = unique(interval))) %>%
  mutate(interval_max = breaks[match(interval, levels(interval)) + 1])

merged_df <- centennial_counts_all %>%
  left_join(datos_cli, by = "interval_max") %>%
  rename( age = interval_max)
```

### 1.4 Holocene Trends in Climatic variables

8.  This code block synthesizes climatic and disturbance predictors with fossil counts into a multi‑panel figure. First, site‑level and regional data are aggregated by centennial intervals to calculate mean anomalies in global mean surface temperature (GMST; panel *p1*) and rates of temperature change (ΔT per 100 years; panel *p2*). Hurricane metrics are then summarized, including average intensity and frequency with associated standard deviations, and plotted as combined bar, step, and ribbon elements (panel *p3*). Finally, categorical states of thermal, hydroclimatic, and hurricane regimes are reorganized into contiguous temporal segments and visualized as labeled rectangles (panel *p4*), providing a nominal classification of climatic phases. The four predictor panels are arranged vertically beneath the fossil count plot (`pr`) to produce a consolidated figure (`combined_plot`) that integrates ecological and climatic signals across the 0–6 ka interval. The visual outcome corresponds to the **Figure 3**. **Reconstruction of regional coral abundance and paleoclimate trends** from the main text and establishes a coherent framework for interpreting temporal associations between coral fossil records, temperature anomalies, and disturbance regimes.

```{r,fig.width=12, fig.height=10,echo=FALSE}

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(patchwork)

p1 <- merged_df %>%
  group_by(age) %>%
  summarise(GMHT_CPS0_30N = mean(GMHT_CPS0_30N, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = GMHT_CPS0_30N, fill = GMHT_CPS0_30N > 0)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#B8860B", "FALSE" = "#0072B2")) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-1.2, 1.2), xlim = c(0, 6)) +
  scale_x_continuous(position = "top", breaks = seq(0, 6)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1.2, color = "black", linewidth = 0.4) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    strip.background = element_blank(),
    panel.background = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "none",
    axis.title.x = element_blank()
  ) +
  labs(y = "GMST(°C)\nanomalies")

p2 <- merged_df %>%
  group_by(age) %>%
  summarise(dT_raw = mean(dT_raw, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = dT_raw, fill = dT_raw > 0)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#E69F00", "FALSE" = "#56B4E9")) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-1.2, 0.7)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    axis.title.x = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.x = element_blank()
  ) +
  labs(y = expression("Rate of Change\nẟT(°C) / 100 yr"))


hur_plot_data <- merged_df %>%
  group_by(age) %>%
  summarise(
    Hur100_av = mean(Hur100_av, na.rm = TRUE),
    Hur100_fqcy = mean(Hur100_fqcy, na.rm = TRUE),
    Hur100_fqcy_sd = sd(Hur100_fqcy, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  arrange(age)

p3 <- ggplot(hur_plot_data, aes(x = age)) +
  geom_col(aes(y = Hur100_av, fill = Hur100_av > 10), alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_step(aes(y = Hur100_fqcy), color = "darkblue", linewidth = 0.8) +
  suppressWarnings(    geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = Hur100_fqcy - Hur100_fqcy_sd,
                    ymax = Hur100_fqcy + Hur100_fqcy_sd),
                fill = "black", alpha = 0.15)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#4D4D4D", "FALSE" = "#999999")) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 50)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    strip.background = element_blank(),
    panel.background = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "none",
    axis.title.x = element_blank()
  ) +
  labs(y = "Hurricane Average\n(events/100 yr)")


df_segments <- merged_df %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(Thermal, Hydro, Hurricane),
               names_to = "variable",
               values_to = "state") %>%
  arrange(variable, age) %>%
  group_by(variable) %>%
  mutate(change = state != lag(state, default = first(state)),
         segment_id = cumsum(change)) %>%
  group_by(variable, state, segment_id) %>%
  summarise(age_start = min(age),
            age_end   = max(age),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(label_x = (age_start + age_end)/2)

df_segments <- df_segments %>%
  group_by(variable) %>%
  arrange(age_start) %>%
  mutate(age_end = lead(age_start, default = max(age_end)))

p4<-ggplot(df_segments) +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = age_start, xmax = age_end,
                ymin = as.numeric(factor(variable)) - 0.4,
                ymax = as.numeric(factor(variable)) + 0.4,
                fill = state)) +
  geom_text(aes(x = label_x,
                y = as.numeric(factor(variable)),
                label = state),
            color = "black", size = 3) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 1:3,
                     labels = levels(factor(df_segments$variable))) +
scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "warmer"   = "#DAA520",
    "cooler"   = "#56B4E9",
    "LIA"      = "#56B4E9",
    "CWP&MWA"  = "#DAA520",
    "wet"      = "#999933",
    "dry"      = "#CCBB44",
    "variable" = "#DDCC77",
    "low"      = "#FFFFFF",
    "medium"   = "#CCCCCC",
    "high"     = "#999999"))+
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")+
  labs(x = "Age (ka)", y = "Nominal Terms")

combined_plot <- pr/ p1 / p2 / p3 / p4 + plot_layout(ncol = 1, heights = c(1,1, 1, 1, 1.2))
combined_plot

ggsave("combined_plot.pdf", plot = combined_plot, width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 300, device = cairo_pdf)
```

### **2. Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)**

To initiate the modelling of climate impacts on acroporid density we start with theory-driven variable selection and data preparation, including **Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)** for autocorrelation checks and to identify colinearities between explanatory and response variables. Although colinearity does not strictly invalidate the GAM process, we exclude redundant variables with a correlation coefficient \> 0.5 to refine the final model.

### 2.1 Variable Correlation

9.  This code block evaluates the relationships among numeric variables in the merged dataset. After isolating all numeric fields and excluding the identifier column, a correlation matrix is computed using complete cases to ensure robustness against missing values. The resulting matrix quantifies pairwise linear associations among climatic, ecological, and disturbance predictors. The `corrplot` function is then employed to visualize the upper triangle of the matrix, displaying correlation coefficients as circles with annotated values. The graphical representation (**Supplementary Figure 1**) highlights the strength and direction of associations, facilitating the identification of potential collinearity or redundancy among predictors prior to statistical modeling.

```{r,fig.width=12, fig.height=10, echo=FALSE}
library(corrplot)
library(ggsignif)

numeric_vars <- merged_df[, sapply(merged_df, is.numeric)]
numeric_vars <- numeric_vars[, !colnames(numeric_vars) %in% "ID"]

cor_matrix <- cor(numeric_vars, use = "complete.obs")

corrplot(cor_matrix, method = "circle", type = "upper",
         tl.col = "black", tl.srt = 45, addCoef.col = "black")
```

**Supplementary Figure 1.** Correlation Plot showing Pearson product–moment correlation coefficients between pairs of numeric variables.

### 2.2 Coral-Climate Interaction Analysis

10. This code block consolidates site‑level and regional density summaries with climatic predictors to generate combined analytical outputs. First, the centennial density results from each locality are merged into a unified dataset (`df_final`) and categorized into panels representing local, zonal, and regional scales. Temporal intervals are standardized into 0.1‑ka bins, ensuring alignment between ecological and climatic records. The merged dataset (`merged_df_c`) incorporates fossil density estimates alongside thermal, hydroclimatic, and hurricane variables, and constructs composite categorical states (`ClimateCombo`) that capture simultaneous climatic conditions. Frequency counts of these combinations are calculated by site, and overall totals are derived to assess distributional balance. Tabular summaries are produced with the `gt` package, reporting frequencies and totals per site, as well as descriptive statistics of density by site‑combo. To ensure analytical robustness, only combinations with at least three observations are retained (`combos_validos`), and the filtered dataset is reordered by median density within panels. The resulting summaries (`resumen_spot` and `resumen_spot_combo`) provide measures of central tendency, dispersion, and extremes for each site and climatic combination. This chunk therefore establishes the integrated framework for evaluating how coral fossil densities vary under distinct climatic regimes across spatial scales.

```{r,echo=FALSE}
library(forcats)

  mutate(panel = case_when(
    spot == "Punta Maroma" ~ "Punta Maroma",
    spot == "Florida" ~ "Florida",
    spot %in% c("Saint Croix",
                "Belize") ~ "Belize & Saint Croix",
    spot == "Regional (All spots)" ~ "Regional"
  ))

  left_join(datos_cli %>% mutate(interval = as.character(interval)), by = "interval") %>%
  rename(density = avg_median, age = interval_mid)

merged_df_c$ClimateCombo <- interaction(merged_df_c$Thermal,
                                      merged_df_c$Hydro,
                                      merged_df_c$Hurricane,
                                      sep = "_")

merged_df_c[!complete.cases(merged_df_c), ]

merged_df_c$ClimateCombo <- reorder(merged_df_c$ClimateCombo,
                                  merged_df_c$density,
                                  median)
NULL

totales %>%

invisible(combo_freq %>% filter(n >= 3))
invisible(combo_freq %>% filter(n < 3))

datos_filtrados <- merged_df_c %>%

datos_filtrados <- datos_filtrados %>%
```

### 2.3 Wilcoxon test (Bonferroni adjustment)

11. This code block provides an assessment of differences in coral fossil density among climatic regimes, highlighting statistically significant contrasts across reef sites. here we implement non‑parametric pairwise comparisons of fossil density across climatic combinations. A custom function (`get_signif_df_v1`) is first defined to perform Wilcoxon rank‑sum tests between all pairs of climatic states within each site, applying Bonferroni correction to control for multiple comparisons. The function returns the test statistics, p‑values, and significance codes, which are then aggregated across sites into a single dataset (`spot_signifs_v1`). Significant results are formatted into a summary table using the `gt` package. A refined version of the function (`get_signif_df`) is subsequently introduced to restrict analyses to combinations with at least three observations, ensuring statistical robustness. This version also calculates annotation positions for graphical overlays. The procedure is applied to each site, and results are merged with panel metadata to facilitate visualization.

```{r,echo=FALSE}
library(dplyr)
library(knitr)

get_signif_df_v1 <- function(df, spot_name){
  pw <- pairwise.wilcox.test(df$density, df$ClimateCombo,
                             p.adjust.method = "bonferroni", exact = FALSE)
  sig_pairs <- which(!is.na(pw$p.value), arr.ind = TRUE)
  signif_code <- function(p){
    if(p < 0.001) return("***")
    else if(p < 0.01) return("**")
    else if(p < 0.05) return("*")
    else return("ns")
  }
  out <- data.frame()
  for(i in seq_len(nrow(sig_pairs))){
    row <- sig_pairs[i,1]; col <- sig_pairs[i,2]
    pval <- pw$p.value[row,col]
    out <- rbind(out, data.frame(
      spot = spot_name,
      group1 = rownames(pw$p.value)[row],
      group2 = colnames(pw$p.value)[col],
      p_value = pval,
      signif = signif_code(pval)
    ))
  }
  return(out)
}

spot_signifs_v1 <- bind_rows(lapply(unique(datos_filtrados$spot), function(p){
  df_spot <- datos_filtrados %>% filter(spot == p)
  get_signif_df_v1(df_spot, p)
}))


spot_signifs_v1 %>% filter(signif != "ns") %>%
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Wilcoxon test (Bonferroni adjustment) ",
    subtitle = "significant results by reef spot"
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(columns = c(p_value, signif),
             decimals = 3)

get_signif_df <- function(df, spot_name){
  combos_validas <- names(which(table(df$ClimateCombo) >= 3))
  df <- df %>% filter(ClimateCombo %in% combos_validas)
  
  if(length(unique(df$ClimateCombo)) < 3){
    return(data.frame())
  }
  
  pw <- pairwise.wilcox.test(df$density, df$ClimateCombo,
                             p.adjust.method = "bonferroni",
                             exact = FALSE)
  
  sig_pairs <- which(pw$p.value < 0.05, arr.ind = TRUE)
  if(nrow(sig_pairs) == 0){
    return(data.frame())
  }
  
  signif_code <- function(p){
    if(p < 0.001) return("***")
    else if(p < 0.01) return("**")
    else if(p < 0.05) return("*")
    else if(p < 0.1) return(".")
    else return("ns")
  }
  
  max_y <- max(df$density, na.rm = TRUE)
  step_y <- max_y * 0.08
  
  out <- data.frame()
  for(i in seq_len(nrow(sig_pairs))){
    row <- sig_pairs[i,1]; col <- sig_pairs[i,2]
    pval <- pw$p.value[row,col]
    out <- rbind(out, data.frame(
      spot = spot_name,
      group1 = rownames(pw$p.value)[row],
      group2 = colnames(pw$p.value)[col],
      annotation = signif_code(pval),  
      y_position = max_y * 1.1 + (i-1) * step_y
    ))
  }
  return(out)
}

spots <- unique(datos_filtrados$spot)

spot_signifs <- bind_rows(lapply(spots, function(p){
  df_spot <- datos_filtrados %>% filter(spot == p)
  get_signif_df(df_spot, p)
}))

panel_map <- datos_filtrados %>% distinct(spot, panel)
spot_signifs <- spot_signifs %>% left_join(panel_map, by = "spot")
```

### 2.4 Coral-climate combo trends (KDE density based)

Next, we continue with the exploratory analysis by detecting combinations of used thermal, hydro climatic and hurricane related variables and how these combinations correlate with the acroporid' density response. 

12. This code block refines the non‑parametric testing framework and integrates the results into a comprehensive figure. A tailored function (`get_signif_df`) is defined to perform pairwise Wilcoxon rank‑sum tests between climatic combinations, applying Bonferroni correction and restricting analyses to combinations with sufficient sample size (≥3 observations). The function returns significant contrasts along with annotation codes and vertical positioning for graphical overlays. These results are aggregated across sites (`spot_signifs`) and linked to panel metadata for visualization. The plotting routine then constructs boxplots of coral fossil density by climatic combination, with jittered points to display individual observations and facets to separate local, zonal, and regional scales. Statistically significant pairwise differences are highlighted directly on the plots using annotated brackets. The `Supplementary Figure 2` is formatted with consistent color schemes, bold axis labels, and a consolidated legend, and exported as a high‑resolution PDF for publication. This chunk thus integrates statistical inference with graphical representation, providing a clear depiction of how coral fossil densities vary across climatic regimes and spatial scales, while explicitly marking significant contrasts.

```{r,fig.width=12, fig.height=10,echo=FALSE}

get_signif_df <- function(df, spot_name){
  combos_validas <- names(which(table(df$ClimateCombo) >= 3))
  df <- df %>% filter(ClimateCombo %in% combos_validas)
  
  if(length(unique(df$ClimateCombo)) < 3){
    return(data.frame())
  }
  
  # Ad-hoc Bonferroni Test 
  pw <- pairwise.wilcox.test(df$density, df$ClimateCombo,
                             p.adjust.method = "bonferroni",
                             exact = FALSE)
  
  sig_pairs <- which(pw$p.value < 0.05, arr.ind = TRUE)
  if(nrow(sig_pairs) == 0){
    return(data.frame())
  }
  
  signif_code <- function(p){
    if(p < 0.001) return("***")
    else if(p < 0.01) return("**")
    else if(p < 0.05) return("*")
    else if(p < 0.1) return(".")
    else return("ns")
  }
  
  max_y <- max(df$density, na.rm = TRUE)
  step_y <- max_y * 0.08
  
  out <- data.frame()
  for(i in seq_len(nrow(sig_pairs))){
    row <- sig_pairs[i,1]; col <- sig_pairs[i,2]
    pval <- pw$p.value[row,col]
    out <- rbind(out, data.frame(
      spot = spot_name,
      group1 = rownames(pw$p.value)[row],
      group2 = colnames(pw$p.value)[col],
      annotation = signif_code(pval),  
      y_position = max_y * 1.1 + (i-1) * step_y
    ))
  }
  return(out)
}

spots <- unique(datos_filtrados$spot)

spot_signifs <- bind_rows(lapply(spots, function(p){
  df_spot <- datos_filtrados %>% filter(spot == p)
  get_signif_df(df_spot, p)
}))

panel_map <- datos_filtrados %>% distinct(spot, panel)
spot_signifs <- spot_signifs %>% left_join(panel_map, by = "spot")



fig3<-suppressWarnings(
  ggplot(datos_filtrados, aes(x = reorder(ClimateCombo, density, FUN = median), y = density, fill = spot)) +
```

**Supplementary Figure 2.** **Boxplots of *A. palmata* densities (population) under Holocene climate combinations.** Highest and lowest acroporid density values both occur under warmer intervals associated with wet conditions and variable hurricane frequency (HF). Whereas the bulk of density values occur under cooler intervals with combinations of frequent hurricanes and wet conditions, or infrequent hurricanes and dry conditions. The densities from these cool scenarios differ significantly from other climate regimes, as shown by ad‑hoc Wilcoxon pairwise comparisons with Bonferroni adjustment (p‑values indicated). Boxes are colored by thermal trends following color code from Figure 1.

## 3. Modelling Coral-Climate (GAMM)

### 3.1 Data preparation

13. This code block prepares the dataset for generalized additive modeling by re‑leveling categorical predictors and structuring site‑specific and regional panels. The climatic variables (`Thermal`, `Hydro`, `Hurricane`) are converted to factors with defined reference states (“warmer,” “wet,” and “low”), ensuring consistent contrasts in subsequent statistical analyses. The dataset is then filtered to retain observations from the four focal reef sites (***Punta Maroma*****, *Florida*, *Belize*, *Saint Croix***), with each assigned to its own panel. A regional dataset is additionally constructed by pooling all sites under the label “**Regional**.” To facilitate count‑based modeling, a constant variable (`counts = 1`) is introduced, representing the presence of each record. Finally, all site‑level and regional subsets are merged into a unified dataset (`merged_df_g`), which provides a standardized structure for comparative modeling of coral fossil densities across spatial scales and climatic regimes.

```{r,echo=FALSE}
library(mgcv)
library(dplyr)
library(patchwork)

merged_df <- merged_df %>%
  mutate(
    Thermal   = relevel(as.factor(Thermal), ref = "warmer"),
    Hydro     = relevel(as.factor(Hydro), ref = "wet"),
    Hurricane = relevel(as.factor(Hurricane), ref = "low")
  )%>%
  filter(spot %in% c("Punta Maroma", "Florida", "Belize", "Saint Croix")) %>%
  mutate(panel = spot)

datos_pm <- merged_df %>% filter(spot == "Punta Maroma")
datos_fl <- merged_df %>% filter(spot == "Florida")
datos_bz <- merged_df %>% filter(spot == "Belize")
datos_sc <- merged_df %>% filter(spot == "Saint Croix")
datos_reg <- merged_df %>%
  filter(spot %in% c("Punta Maroma", "Florida", "Belize", "Saint Croix")) %>%
  mutate(spot = "Regional")

merged_df <- merged_df %>%
   mutate(counts = 1)

merged_df_g <- bind_rows(datos_pm, datos_fl, datos_bz, datos_sc, datos_reg)

```

### 3.2 GAM analysis

### Data preparation (normalization)

14. This code block normalizes fossil counts across sites and constructs the final dataset for comparative modeling. A custom function (`normalize_counts`) is defined to scale raw counts relative to the maximum within each panel, producing standardized values (`counts_norm`). To address boundary cases where normalized values equal 0 or 1, a small‑sample variance correction is applied (`counts_norm_sv`), ensuring statistical stability. The dataset is then partitioned by site (***Punta Maroma*****, *Florida*, *Belize*, *Saint Croix***) and aggregated by centennial age bins, with associated climatic and disturbance predictors summarized as means. Each subset is normalized and labeled with its respective panel name. A regional dataset is additionally created by pooling all sites, normalized in the same manner, and explicitly tagged as “**Regional**.” Finally, all site‑level and regional subsets are merged into a consolidated dataset (`merged_df_g`), which provides harmonized counts and predictor variables for subsequent generalized additive modeling and comparative analyses.

```{r,echo=FALSE}

normalize_counts <- function(df, panel_name){
  df %>%
    mutate(
      counts_norm = round(counts / max(counts, na.rm = TRUE), 4),
      # aplicar SV si hay 0 o 1
      counts_norm_sv = ifelse(counts_norm %in% c(0,1),
                              ((counts_norm * (n() - 1)) + 0.5) / n(),
                              counts_norm),
      panel = panel_name
    )
}

datos_pm <- merged_df %>%
  filter(spot == "Punta Maroma") %>%
  group_by(age) %>%
  summarise(
    counts = sum(counts, na.rm = TRUE), 
    Hur100_av = mean(Hur100_av, na.rm = TRUE),
    Hur100_fqcy = mean(Hur100_fqcy, na.rm = TRUE),
    GMHT_CPS0_30N = mean(GMHT_CPS0_30N, na.rm = TRUE),
    dT_raw = mean(dT_raw, na.rm = TRUE),
    Hydro = first(Hydro),
    Thermal = first(Thermal),
    Hurricane = first(Hurricane),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  normalize_counts("Punta Maroma")

datos_fl <- merged_df %>%
  filter(spot == "Florida") %>%
  group_by(age) %>%
  summarise(
    counts = sum(counts, na.rm = TRUE), 
    Hur100_av = mean(Hur100_av, na.rm = TRUE),
    Hur100_fqcy = mean(Hur100_fqcy, na.rm = TRUE),
    GMHT_CPS0_30N = mean(GMHT_CPS0_30N, na.rm = TRUE),
    dT_raw = mean(dT_raw, na.rm = TRUE),
    Hydro = first(Hydro),
    Thermal = first(Thermal),
    Hurricane = first(Hurricane),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  normalize_counts("Florida")

datos_bz <- merged_df %>%
  filter(spot == "Belize") %>%
  group_by(age) %>%
  summarise(
    counts = sum(counts, na.rm = TRUE), 
    Hur100_av = mean(Hur100_av, na.rm = TRUE),
    Hur100_fqcy = mean(Hur100_fqcy, na.rm = TRUE),
    GMHT_CPS0_30N = mean(GMHT_CPS0_30N, na.rm = TRUE),
    dT_raw = mean(dT_raw, na.rm = TRUE),
    Hydro = first(Hydro),
    Thermal = first(Thermal),
    Hurricane = first(Hurricane),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  normalize_counts("Belize")

datos_sc <- merged_df %>%
  filter(spot == "Saint Croix") %>%
  group_by(age) %>%
  summarise(
    counts = sum(counts, na.rm = TRUE), 
    Hur100_av = mean(Hur100_av, na.rm = TRUE),
    Hur100_fqcy = mean(Hur100_fqcy, na.rm = TRUE),
    GMHT_CPS0_30N = mean(GMHT_CPS0_30N, na.rm = TRUE),
    dT_raw = mean(dT_raw, na.rm = TRUE),
    Hydro = first(Hydro),
    Thermal = first(Thermal),
    Hurricane = first(Hurricane),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%

datos_reg <- merged_df %>%
  filter(spot %in% c("Punta Maroma", "Florida", "Belize", "Saint Croix")) %>%
  group_by(age) %>%
  summarise(
    counts = sum(counts, na.rm = TRUE),   
    Hur100_av = mean(Hur100_av, na.rm = TRUE),
    Hur100_fqcy = mean(Hur100_fqcy, na.rm = TRUE),
    GMHT_CPS0_30N = mean(GMHT_CPS0_30N, na.rm = TRUE),
    dT_raw = mean(dT_raw, na.rm = TRUE),
    Hydro = first(Hydro),
    Thermal = first(Thermal),

merged_df_g <- bind_rows(datos_pm, datos_fl, datos_bz, datos_sc, datos_reg)
```

Because of our interest in assessing temporal trends in continuous variables (e.g., temperature, hurricane frequency), we employ a **Beta regression family** with a **logit link function** and **regression splines**. This family regression distribution also responds to the inherent properties of the selected response variable which is bounded between 0 and 1. Finally, we define reference baselines for the thermal and hydro climatic predictors and set the model baseline to conditions 'warmer' than the 18th-century average, 'wet' hydro climatic periods, and 'calm' hurricane intervals. By establishing these baselines, we enable the model to accurately capture the effects of known periods of heightened climate variability, such as the Little Ice Age or the Caribbean Warm Period in concordance with our goals.

Model performance analysis encompassed a step-wise approach. Prior to model fitting, each site‑specific dataset was screened for detecting and suppressing statistical outliers in coral density and mean hurricane intensity. To that, we use Tukey’s interquartile range criterion. Filtering and removing outliers helps minimizing undue influence of extreme values and improve model stability. After outliers’ filtering, we assess the marginal effect of each potential explanatory variable by constructing seven univariate GAMs to evaluate independent, isolated effects. Subsequently, we built a suite of multivariate GAMs to assess the conditional, combined effects of variables in the presence of increasing numbers of variables and variable interactions.

To identify the optimal configuration in both cases, we applied a competitive **Akaike Information Criterion threshold (∆AIC \<2)** alongside the principle of model parsimony. Upon selecting the overall optimal configuration, we conduct a rigorous quality assessment, including residual analysis, accuracy testing, and cross-validation for model stability. 

#### 3.2.1 Evaluating marginal effects. Results.

To test the degree of concordance between local *A. palmata* population trajectories and regional climate trends, we first investigate the explanatory power of climatic predictor marginal (isolated) effects of both types, smooth and linear. When evaluating these marginal effects, models indicate temperature anomalies and centennial hurricane average impacts metrics along with thermal and Hydrodynamics trends where helpful indicators of coral density responses. As such, explained deviances yield values between 0.4 (regional) -90% (Punta Maroma, Mx)(**Suppl. Material 1, Supp. Table 1, Supp.Fig.1**). Nevertheless, biological organisms are influenced by the synergistic interplay of multiple climatic factors rather than isolated variables, so we next explore the combined effects following same approach.  

15. Next three code blocks implement generalized additive models (GAMs) to evaluate the marginal effects of climatic and disturbance predictors on normalized coral fossil densities. A set of candidate formulas (`formulas_mg`) is defined, each incorporating age and a single predictor (temperature anomalies, rates of change, hurricane frequency and averages, or categorical climatic states). A helper function (`fit_gams_panel`) fits GAMs for each formula within a given panel using a beta regression with logit link, while `compare_gams` extracts Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) values, computes ΔAIC relative to the best model, and derives model weights. The procedure is applied across all panels (local sites and regional aggregate), and results are consolidated into `stats_all`. Tabular summaries are generated with the `gt` package, and diagnostic plots display ΔAIC values and model weights, with a dashed threshold line (ΔAIC = 2) indicating competitive models. A refined function (`fit_best_gam`) is then introduced to fit, summarize, and extract key statistics from the best‑performing models at each site, including explained deviance, adjusted R², significant terms, and effective degrees of freedom. The outputs are compiled into a comparison table and exported as a publication‑ready PDF, while supplementary figures visualize relative model performance. This chunk thus provides a systematic framework for model selection and interpretation, identifying the most influential climatic and disturbance predictors of coral fossil density across spatial scales.

```{r setup-formulas, echo=FALSE}
formulas_mg <- list(
  M_temp = counts_norm_sv ~ s(age) + s(GMHT_CPS0_30N),
  M_dt   = counts_norm_sv ~ s(age) + s(dT_raw),          
  M_hf   = counts_norm_sv ~ s(age) + s(Hur100_fqcy),
  M_hav  = counts_norm_sv ~ s(age) + s(Hur100_av),
  M_the  = counts_norm_sv ~ s(age) + Thermal,
  M_hyd  = counts_norm_sv ~ s(age) + Hydro,
  M_hur  = counts_norm_sv ~ s(age) + Hurricane
)

fit_gams_panel <- function(data, formulas) {
  lapply(formulas, function(f)
    gam(f, data = data, family = betar(link = "logit"), method = "REML"))
}

compare_gams <- function(fits) {
  stats <- lapply(fits, AIC)
  df <- data.frame(Model = names(stats), AIC = unlist(stats))
  df <- df %>%
    mutate(deltaAIC = AIC - min(AIC),
           weight = exp(-0.5 * deltaAIC) / sum(exp(-0.5 * deltaAIC)))
  return(df)
}
```

**Suppl. Table 1. Explained coral climate interaction within univariate GAM settings:** definition and relative marginal effect (measured as Chi.sq) and statistical significance (p-value, Pr(\>\|z\|)) of the relevant climate variables on *A. palmata* population trajectory response.

```{r best-gams, echo=FALSE}
library(broom)

fit_best_gam <- function(formula, data, model_name, segment_name, outdir = "gam_outputs") {
  gam_model <- gam(
    formula = formula,
    data = data,
    family = betar(link = "logit"),
    method = "REML"
  )
  
  cat("\n============================\n")
  cat("Best GAM for", segment_name, "-", model_name, "\n")
  cat("============================\n")
  print(summary(gam_model))
  
  gam_summary <- summary(gam_model)
  
  tidy_terms <- broom::tidy(gam_model) %>%
    filter(p.value < 0.05) %>%
    select(term, p.value)
  
  edf_info <- gam_summary$s.table
  edf_terms <- paste0(rownames(edf_info), " (EDF=", round(edf_info[,"edf"],2), ")")
  
  summary_df <- data.frame(
    Segment = segment_name,
    Model   = model_name,
    AIC     = AIC(gam_model),
    DevianceExplained = gam_summary$dev.expl,
    R2_Adj  = gam_summary$r.sq,
    SignificantTerms  = paste(tidy_terms$term, collapse = "; "),
    EDF_Terms = paste(edf_terms, collapse = "; ")
  )
  
  return(list(model = gam_model, summary = summary_df))
}
```

**Explained coral climate interaction within univariate GAM settings:** definition and relative marginal effect (measured as Chi.sq) and statistical significance (p-value, Pr(\>\|z\|)) of the relevant climate variables on *A. palmata* population trajectory response.

### 3.3 GAMM combined effects analysis

To capture the compounded effects of climatic factors on the acroporid population trajectory, we constructed a series of multivariate GAMMs incorporating interactions among variables **(Suppl. Table 2).**

16. This chunk thus establishes the methodological framework for testing additive and interactive influences of multiple climatic drivers on coral fossil density across temporal and spatial scales. This code block outlines the construction of increasingly complex generalized additive mixed models (GAMMs) to evaluate joint effects of climatic and disturbance predictors on normalized coral fossil densities. A structured table (`model_table`) is created to document the progression of models, beginning with a base formulation that includes only age (M1), and sequentially adding predictors such as global mean surface temperature anomalies (GMHT_CPS0_30N), rates of temperature change (dT_raw), hurricane frequency (Hur100_fqcy), hurricane averages (Hur100_av), and categorical climatic states (Hydro, Thermal, Hurricane). Two parallel branches are defined: one incorporating hurricane frequency and the other hurricane averages, each expanded stepwise to include hydroclimatic and thermal predictors. The resulting table provides a transparent design of nested model complexity, facilitating systematic comparison of marginal and joint effects.

**Suppl. Table 2. Design of increasingly complex sequence of joint GAM versions.** Eight versions of GAM models used to evaluate the combined effects of climatic variables on *Acropora palmata* coral density response. The sequence begins with the simplest model considering only age as a baseline and progressively adds other predictors one at a time. Two parallel branches were constructed: one incorporating the 100‑yr hurricane frequency (Hur100_fqcy) and another incorporating the 100‑yr hurricane impact average (Hur100_av). This design avoids including both hurricane metrics simultaneously, ensuring interpretability of marginal and joint effects.

17. This chunk thus establishes a rigorous framework for evaluating additive and joint influences of climatic anomalies, rates of change, and disturbance regimes on coral fossil density, while ensuring model stability across datasets of varying size. Here we implement a sequence of increasingly complex generalized additive models (GAMs) to evaluate joint effects of climatic and disturbance predictors on normalized coral fossil densities. Two parallel branches are defined: one incorporating hurricane frequency (`Hur100_fqcy`) and the other hurricane averages (`Hur100_av`), each progressively expanded to include hydroclimatic and thermal predictors, culminating in full models with all three disturbance categories. A custom function (`fit_combined_gams_safe`) is introduced to fit these models robustly across panels. The function applies data cleaning, selects appropriate fitting strategies (`bam` for larger panels, `gam` for smaller datasets), and includes fallback to quasibinomial regression when beta regression fails. Model summaries are extracted, including AIC, deviance explained, adjusted R², and effective degrees of freedom. Comparative statistics are computed, with ΔAIC and model weights used to assess relative support. Diagnostic plots visualize ΔAIC values (with a dashed threshold at ΔAIC = 2) and AIC weights, highlighting competitive models. The procedure is applied to site‑specific panels (***Punta Maroma*****, *Florida*, *Belize***) and the regional aggregate, producing structured outputs (`results_pm`, `results_fl`, `results_bz`, `results_reg`).

```{r, echo=FALSE}

formulas_cb <- list(
  # Base
  M1 = counts_norm_sv ~ s(age),
  M2 = counts_norm_sv ~ s(age) + s(GMHT_CPS0_30N),
  M3 = counts_norm_sv ~ s(age) + s(GMHT_CPS0_30N) + s(dT_raw),
  # increasing complexy using Hur100_fqcy predictor
  M4_fqcy = counts_norm_sv ~ s(age) + s(GMHT_CPS0_30N) + s(dT_raw) + s(Hur100_fqcy),
  M5_fqcy = counts_norm_sv ~ s(age) + s(GMHT_CPS0_30N) + s(dT_raw) + s(Hur100_fqcy) + Hydro,
  M6_fqcy = counts_norm_sv ~ s(age) + s(GMHT_CPS0_30N) + s(dT_raw) + s(Hur100_fqcy) + Hydro + Thermal,
  M7_fqcy = counts_norm_sv ~ s(age) + s(GMHT_CPS0_30N) + s(dT_raw) + s(Hur100_fqcy) + Hydro + Thermal + Hurricane,
  # increasing complexy using Hur100_av predictor 
  M4_av = counts_norm_sv ~ s(age) + s(GMHT_CPS0_30N) + s(dT_raw) + s(Hur100_av),
  M5_av = counts_norm_sv ~ s(age) + s(GMHT_CPS0_30N) + s(dT_raw) + s(Hur100_av) + Hydro,
  M6_av = counts_norm_sv ~ s(age) + s(GMHT_CPS0_30N) + s(dT_raw) + s(Hur100_av) + Hydro + Thermal,
  M7_av = counts_norm_sv ~ s(age) + s(GMHT_CPS0_30N) + s(dT_raw) + s(Hur100_av) + Hydro + Thermal + Hurricane
)

## --- Safety helpers (added) -------------------------------------------
## Fitting the full combined formulas (up to 4 smooth terms, default k = 10
## each) on small panels such as Saint Croix requires far more unique
## covariate values than a handful of centennial bins can provide. Letting
## mgcv build an over-parameterized basis on so little data is the most
## likely cause of the session crashes reported for that site. These
## helpers (i) cap the basis dimension `k` of every smooth term to a value
## that is safe given the panel size, and (ii) skip formulas that are
## clearly over-parameterized for the panel rather than attempting to fit
## them at all.
count_smooth_terms <- function(formula) {
  lengths(regmatches(paste(deparse(formula, width.cutoff = 500L), collapse = " "),
                      gregexpr("s\\(", paste(deparse(formula, width.cutoff = 500L), collapse = " "))))
}

cap_smooth_k <- function(formula, k_max) {
  f_chr <- paste(deparse(formula, width.cutoff = 500L), collapse = " ")
  f_chr <- gsub("s\\(\\s*([A-Za-z0-9_\\.]+)\\s*\\)",
                paste0("s(\\1, k = ", k_max, ")"), f_chr)
  as.formula(f_chr)
}

safe_k_for <- function(n_obs, n_smooth_terms) {
  max(3, min(10, floor((n_obs - 1) / max(1, n_smooth_terms))))
}
## ------------------------------------------------------------------------

fit_combined_gams_safe <- function(formulas_cb, data, segment_name) {
  
  # 🔧 Limpieza previa
  data_clean <- data %>%
    mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~replace(., is.infinite(.), NA))) %>%
    drop_na()
  
  n_obs <- nrow(data_clean)
  
  fits <- lapply(names(formulas_cb), function(name) {
    f <- formulas_cb[[name]]
    n_smooth <- count_smooth_terms(f)

    # Skip formulas that are clearly over-parameterized for this panel
    # instead of letting mgcv attempt a rank-deficient / ill-posed basis.
    if (n_obs < 8 || n_obs <= n_smooth * 3) {
      message(paste("Skipping model", name, "for", segment_name,
                    "- insufficient observations (n =", n_obs, ") for",
                    n_smooth, "smooth term(s)"))
      return(NULL)
    }

    k_max <- safe_k_for(n_obs, n_smooth)
    f_safe <- if (n_smooth > 0) cap_smooth_k(f, k_max) else f

    tryCatch({
      if (n_obs > 100) {
        # Paneles grandes → bam
        bam(f_safe, data = data_clean, family = betar(link = "logit"),
            method = "fREML", select = TRUE, discrete = TRUE)
      } else {
        # Paneles pequeños → gam con k reducido (capped above)
        gam(f_safe, data = data_clean,
            family = betar(link = "logit"), method = "REML",
            select = TRUE)
      }
    }, error = function(e) {
      message(paste("⚠️ Modelo", name, "falló en", segment_name, 
                    "con betar:", e$message, "→ probando quasibinomial"))
      tryCatch({
        gam(f_safe, data = data_clean,
            family = quasibinomial(link = "logit"), method = "REML",
            select = TRUE)
      }, error = function(e2) {
        message(paste("❌ Modelo", name, "falló también con quasibinomial en", segment_name, ":", e2$message))
        return(NULL)
      })
    })
  })
  names(fits) <- names(formulas_cb)
  
  # Filtrar solo los modelos que sí corrieron
  fits <- fits[!sapply(fits, is.null)]
  
  stats <- lapply(names(fits), function(name) {
    m <- fits[[name]]
    s <- summary(m)
    data.frame(
      Model = name,   
      AIC = tryCatch(AIC(m), error = function(e) NA),
      DevianceExplained = s$dev.expl,
      R2_Adj = s$r.sq,
      EDF = sum(m$edf),
      Segment = segment_name,
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    )
  })
  
  stats_df <- bind_rows(stats)
  if (nrow(stats_df) > 0) {
    stats_df <- stats_df %>%
      mutate(deltaAIC = AIC - min(AIC, na.rm = TRUE),
             weight = exp(-0.5 * deltaAIC) / sum(exp(-0.5 * deltaAIC), na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
      arrange(AIC)
  }
  
  # 🔧 Plots (solo si hay stats)
  if (nrow(stats_df) > 0) {
    p_delta <- ggplot(stats_df, aes(x = reorder(Model, deltaAIC), y = deltaAIC)) +
      geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
      geom_hline(yintercept = 2, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
      coord_flip() +
      labs(title = paste("ΔAIC by model -", segment_name),
           subtitle = "Dashed line = ΔAIC = 2 (competitive threshold)",
           x = "Model", y = "ΔAIC") +
      theme_minimal() +
      theme(legend.position = "bottom")
    
    p_weight <- ggplot(stats_df, aes(x = reorder(Model, -weight), y = weight)) +
      geom_col(fill = "darkgreen") +
      coord_flip() +
      labs(title = paste("AIC weights by model -", segment_name),
           subtitle = "Relative probability each model is best",
           x = "Model", y = "AIC weight") +
      theme_minimal()
    
    plots <- list(delta = p_delta, weight = p_weight)
  } else {
    plots <- NULL
  }
  
  return(list(fits = fits, stats = stats_df, plots = plots))
}

datos_pm <- merged_df_g %>% filter(panel == "Punta Maroma")
results_pm <- fit_combined_gams_safe(formulas_cb, datos_pm, "Punta Maroma")

datos_fl <- merged_df_g %>% filter(panel == "Florida")
results_fl <- fit_combined_gams_safe(formulas_cb, datos_fl, "Florida")

datos_bz <- merged_df_g %>% filter(panel == "Belize")
results_bz <- fit_combined_gams_safe(formulas_cb, datos_bz, "Belize")

datos_sc <- merged_df_g %>% filter(panel == "Saint Croix")
results_sc <- fit_combined_gams_safe(formulas_cb, datos_sc, "Saint Croix")

datos_reg <- merged_df_g %>% filter(panel == "Regional")
results_reg <- fit_combined_gams_safe(formulas_cb, datos_reg, "Regional")

```

### 3.4 Model performance & selection

18. This chunk thus completes the comparative modeling workflow, offering a transparent assessment of which climatic and disturbance predictors most strongly explain coral fossil density patterns across reef sites. Here we consolidate the results of the combined GAM analyses across sites into a unified comparison framework. Model statistics from *Punta Maroma*, *Florida*, *Belize*, and the regional aggregate are merged (`comparison_cb_full`), and models within the competitive threshold (ΔAIC ≤ 2) are identified (`competitive_models`). These competitive models are summarized in a formatted table using the `gt` package, reporting AIC, ΔAIC, effective degrees of freedom, deviance explained, adjusted R², and model weights. Two complementary plots are then generated: one displaying ΔAIC values by model across segments, with a dashed line marking the competitive threshold, and another showing AIC weights as relative probabilities of each model being the best fit. Both plots are faceted by site to highlight spatial differences in model performance. The combined figure (`sup_fig2`) provides a clear visual synthesis of model selection outcomes across local and regional scales, and is exported as a high‑resolution supplementary figure.

```{r,fig.width=12, fig.height=10,echo=FALSE}

 # %>%
```

### 4. Models' Quality Control

### 4.1 Parsimony analysis Results

Parsimony analysis highlights that site-specific models incorporating climatic and disturbance predictors yield strong explanatory strength, identifiying clear site-specific differences in model performance. However, regional aggregation dilutes that effect with multiple models competing to achieve a good explanatory signal. At **Punta Maroma**, Model M4_av was favored (Deviance Explained = 0.82, R²_adj = 0.70, weight = 0.69), indicating that hurricane impact average combined with age and climatic predictors yields the most parsimonious fit. In **Florida**, Model M7_av dominated (Deviance Explained = 0.76, R²_adj = 0.64, weight = 0.95), underscoring the importance of including multiple climatic and disturbance variables

For **Belize**, several models competed within the ΔAIC ≤ 2 threshold, but Model M6_fqcy was slightly preferred (Deviance Explained = 0.77, R²_adj = 0.57, weight = 0.28). Other candidates (M7_av, M7_fqcy, M6_av) showed comparable explanatory capacity (Deviance Explained ≈ 0.68–0.70), reflecting moderate but dispersed signal strength. In contrast, the **Regional aggregation** favored Model M7_av (Deviance Explained = 0.65, R²_adj = 0.47, weight = 0.89), though explanatory power remained weaker than localized fits.

**Suppl. Table 3.** **Combined Generalised Additive Models within competitive threshold (ΔAIC ≤ 2) across reef sites and the regional scope.** Reported values include Akaike Information Criterion (AIC), explained deviance, adjusted R2, effective degrees of freedom (EDF), and model weights. Results highlight strong site-specific fits in Florida, Punta Maroma, Mx and Saint Croix, moderate explanatory power in Belize and negligible performance for multiple regional models

This table provides a concise overview of the most parsimonious models across local and regional panels. A complementary scatterplot is then generated, plotting AIC against EDF for each competitive model, with points colored by segment and annotated with model identifiers. This visualization highlights the trade‑off between model fit and complexity, allowing direct comparison of explanatory power versus parsimony across sites. Together, the table and plot establish a clear methodological basis for selecting models that balance statistical performance with ecological interpretability.

### 4.2 Model validation

#### 4.2.1 5-Fold Cross validation Results (Marginal effects)

The cross-validation of marginal models revealed that marginal models capture local correlations but lack stable predictive capacity across folds. Model stability is highly dependent on data quality and resolution, with regional aggregation offering the only panel that sustains a weak, but positive explanatory signal.

The five‑fold cross‑validation revealed highly variable and often unstable signals across sites. In **Belize**, performance fluctuated dramatically: while one fold achieved very high fit (R² ≈ 0.99, Deviance Explained ≈ 0.88), the average across folds was modest (mean R² = 0.29, mean Deviance Explained = −0.13), reflecting inconsistency and limited generalization. **Florida** was consistently weak, with low R² (mean = 0.13) and strongly negative Deviance Explained (mean = −1.93), indicating that models failed to outperform a simple mean‑based prediction.

At **Punta Maroma**, with its high-resolution sampling database, results were particularly erratic: one fold showed strong fit (R² ≈ 0.79, Deviance Explained ≈ 0.71), yet others collapsed with extreme negative Deviance Explained (down to −22.8), yielding an unstable average (mean R² = 0.29, mean Deviance Explained = −7.15). In contrast, the **Regional panel** maintained the most consistent though modest performance, with positive Deviance Explained in several folds and an overall mean R² = 0.30, mean Deviance Explained = 0.11.

20. This code block evaluates the predictive performance of the selected GAM formulation using k‑fold cross‑validation. The dataset is restricted to the four focal panels (***Punta Maroma*****, *Florida*, *Belize*, and *Regional***), and partitioned into five folds. For each fold, the model (`bam`) is trained on the remaining data and tested on the held‑out subset, with predictions generated for normalized fossil counts. Performance metrics are calculated per panel, including fold‑specific R2 values and deviance explained, providing measures of model fit and generalizability. Results are aggregated into `cv_summary_by_panel` for individual folds and `cv_summary_avg` for mean and standard deviation across folds. Both summaries are formatted into publication‑ready tables using the `gt` package. This procedure ensures that model evaluation accounts for variability across panels and folds, offering a robust assessment of predictive reliability and stability of the GAM framework.

```{r,echo=FALSE}
library(mgcv)
library(caret)

set.seed(123)

df_cv <- merged_df_g %>%
  filter(panel %in% c("Punta Maroma", "Florida", "Belize", "Regional"))

folds <- createFolds(df_cv$panel, k = 5)

cv_results <- lapply(seq_along(folds), function(i) {
  test_idx <- folds[[i]]
  train_data <- df_cv[-test_idx, ]
  test_data  <- df_cv[test_idx, ]
  
  m <- bam(counts_norm_sv ~ s(age) + s(Hur100_av),
           data = train_data, family = betar(link="logit"),
           method = "fREML", discrete = TRUE)
  
  preds <- predict(m, newdata = test_data, type = "response")
  
  test_data %>%
    mutate(preds = preds) %>%
    group_by(panel) %>%
    summarise(
      fold = i,
      R2 = cor(counts_norm_sv, preds)^2,
      DevianceExpl = 1 - (sum((counts_norm_sv - preds)^2) /
                            sum((counts_norm_sv - mean(counts_norm_sv))^2)),
      .groups = "drop"
    )
})

cv_summary_by_panel <- bind_rows(cv_results)

cv_summary_avg <- cv_summary_by_panel %>%
  group_by(panel) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_R2 = mean(R2, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_R2   = sd(R2, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_DevianceExpl = mean(DevianceExpl, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_DevianceExpl   = sd(DevianceExpl, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

cv_summary_by_panel %>%
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Cross-validation results by panel",
    subtitle = "Fold-specific R² and Deviance Explained"
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(R2, DevianceExpl),
    decimals = 3
  )

cv_summary_avg %>%
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Average cross-validation results by panel",
    subtitle = "Mean ± SD of R² and Deviance Explained across folds"
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(mean_R2, sd_R2, mean_DevianceExpl, sd_DevianceExpl),
    decimals = 3
  )
```

21. This code block expands the cross‑validation framework to evaluate the predictive performance of marginal GAMs, each incorporating age and a single climatic or disturbance predictor. Five candidate formulas are defined (`formulas_marg`), including models with age alone, age plus global mean surface temperature anomalies (GMHT_CPS0_30N), rates of temperature change (ΔT), hurricane averages, and hurricane frequency. The dataset is partitioned into five folds, and for each fold, models are trained on the remaining data and tested on the held‑out subset. Predictions are generated for normalized fossil counts, and performance metrics are calculated per panel and per model, including fold‑specific R2 values and deviance explained. Results are aggregated into `cv_summary_marginal` for individual folds and `cv_summary_avg_marg` for mean and standard deviation across folds. Both detailed and averaged results are formatted into tables using the `gt` package, providing a transparent comparison of predictive reliability across sites and predictors. This procedure systematically assesses the relative explanatory power of individual climatic variables, establishing their marginal contributions to coral fossil density dynamics.

```{r,echo=FALSE}
set.seed(123)

df_cv <- merged_df_g %>%
  filter(panel %in% c("Punta Maroma", "Florida", "Belize", "Regional"))

folds <- createFolds(df_cv$panel, k = 5)

formulas_marg <- list(
  M_age      = counts_norm_sv ~ s(age),
  M_GMHT     = counts_norm_sv ~ s(age) + s(GMHT_CPS0_30N),
  M_dT       = counts_norm_sv ~ s(age) + s(dT_raw),
  M_Hur_av   = counts_norm_sv ~ s(age) + s(Hur100_av),
  M_Hur_fqcy = counts_norm_sv ~ s(age) + s(Hur100_fqcy)
)

cv_results <- lapply(seq_along(folds), function(i) {
  test_idx <- folds[[i]]
  train_data <- df_cv[-test_idx, ]
  test_data  <- df_cv[test_idx, ]
  
  lapply(names(formulas_marg), function(mname) {
    f <- formulas_marg[[mname]]
    m <- tryCatch(
      bam(f, data = train_data, family = betar(link="logit"),

    )
    
    if (!is.null(m)) {
      preds <- predict(m, newdata = test_data, type = "response")
      
      test_data %>%
        mutate(preds = preds) %>%
        group_by(panel) %>%
        summarise(
          fold = i,
          model = mname,
          R2 = cor(counts_norm_sv, preds)^2,
          DevianceExpl = 1 - (sum((counts_norm_sv - preds)^2) /
                                sum((counts_norm_sv - mean(counts_norm_sv))^2)),
          .groups = "drop"
        )
    } else {
      NULL
    }
  }) %>% bind_rows()
})

cv_summary_marginal <- bind_rows(cv_results)

cv_summary_avg_marg <- cv_summary_marginal %>%
  group_by(panel, model) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_R2 = mean(R2, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_R2   = sd(R2, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_DevianceExpl = mean(DevianceExpl, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_DevianceExpl   = sd(DevianceExpl, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

cv_summary_marginal %>%
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Cross-validation results (marginal models)",
    subtitle = "Fold-specific R² and Deviance Explained by panel and model"
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(R2, DevianceExpl),
    decimals = 3
  )

cv_summary_avg_marg %>%
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Average cross-validation results (marginal models)",
    subtitle = "Mean ± SD of R² and Deviance Explained across folds"
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(mean_R2, sd_R2, mean_DevianceExpl, sd_DevianceExpl),
```

#### 4.2.2 5-Fold Cross validation Results (Combined effects)

The cross‑validation of combined GAMs revealed a more nuanced but still unstable pattern across sites and confirm that while combined models can capture complex climatic signals, their stability is highly site‑dependent. Regional aggregation sustains modest but positive generalization, whereas localized panels (especially **Florida** and **Punta Maroma**) remain vulnerable to overfitting and inconsistent predictive capacity.

In **Belize**, several folds reached very high R² values (up to ≈ 0.98) with positive deviance explained, yet averages across models remained modest (mean R² ≈ 0.25–0.45) and deviance explained often negative. This reflects occasional strong fits but poor consistency across folds.

**Florida** showed gradual improvement in R² with model complexity (mean R² rising from ≈ 0.05 in M1 to ≈ 0.48 in M7_av), but deviance explained remained negative across all models (≈ −1.6 to −1.9), confirming weak generalization beyond the training subsets.

At **Punta Maroma**, some folds produced high R² (up to ≈ 0.84 in M7_av), but averages were undermined by strongly negative deviance explained (≈ −4 to −7 across models), highlighting instability and overfitting tendencies.

In contrast, the **Regional** panel maintained the most consistent signal: mean R² increased steadily with model complexity (≈ 0.25 in M1 to ≈ 0.43 in M7_av), and deviance explained turned positive in the hurricane‑average branch (M4–M7_av, mean deviance explained ≈ 0.17–0.31). This indicates that regional aggregation, while weaker than localized fits, was the only context where combined models achieved reproducible explanatory strength.

23. This code block extends the cross‑validation framework to the full set of combined GAMs, incorporating multiple climatic and disturbance predictors simultaneously. The dataset is restricted to the four focal panels (***Punta Maroma*****, *Florida*, *Belize*, and *Regional***), and partitioned into five folds. For each fold, all candidate combined models (`formulas_cb`) are fitted using beta regression with logit link, and predictions are generated for the held‑out subset. Performance metrics are calculated per panel and per model, including fold‑specific R2 values and deviance explained, providing measures of predictive accuracy and model fit. Results are aggregated into `cv_summary_combined` for individual folds and `cv_summary_avg` for mean values across folds. Both detailed and averaged results are formatted into tables with the `gt` package, offering a clear comparison of predictive reliability across sites and models. This procedure provides a rigorous assessment of how joint climatic and disturbance predictors improve explanatory power relative to marginal models, highlighting differences in predictive performance across reef sites and the regional aggregate.

```{r,echo=FALSE}
library(mgcv)
library(caret)
library(dplyr)

set.seed(123)

df_cv <- merged_df_g %>%
  filter(panel %in% c("Punta Maroma", "Florida", "Belize", "Saint Croix", "Regional"))

folds <- createFolds(df_cv$panel, k = 5)

cv_results <- lapply(seq_along(folds), function(i) {
  test_idx <- folds[[i]]
  train_data <- df_cv[-test_idx, ]
  test_data  <- df_cv[test_idx, ]
  
  lapply(names(formulas_cb), function(mname) {
    f <- formulas_cb[[mname]]
    n_smooth <- count_smooth_terms(f)
    train_panel <- unique(train_data$panel)
    n_obs_train <- nrow(train_data)

    # Skip / cap basis dimension per fold to avoid over-parameterized,
    # potentially crash-prone fits on small training folds (e.g. Saint Croix).
    if (n_obs_train <= n_smooth * 3) return(NULL)
    k_max <- safe_k_for(n_obs_train, n_smooth)
    f_safe <- if (n_smooth > 0) cap_smooth_k(f, k_max) else f

    m <- tryCatch(
      bam(f_safe, data = train_data, family = betar(link="logit"),
          method = "fREML", discrete = TRUE),
      error = function(e) NULL
    )
    
    if (!is.null(m)) {
      preds <- predict(m, newdata = test_data, type = "response")
      
      test_data %>%
        mutate(preds = preds) %>%
        group_by(panel) %>%
        summarise(
          fold = i,
          model = mname,
          R2 = cor(counts_norm_sv, preds)^2,
          DevianceExpl = 1 - (sum((counts_norm_sv - preds)^2) /
                                sum((counts_norm_sv - mean(counts_norm_sv))^2)),
          .groups = "drop"
        )
    } else {
      NULL
    }
  }) %>% bind_rows()
})

cv_summary_combined <- bind_rows(cv_results)

cv_summary_avg <- cv_summary_combined %>%
  group_by(panel, model) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_R2 = mean(R2, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_DevianceExpl = mean(DevianceExpl, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

cv_summary_combined %>%
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Cross-validation results (combined models)",
    subtitle = "Fold-specific R² and Deviance Explained by panel and model"
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(R2, DevianceExpl),
    decimals = 3
  )

cv_summary_avg %>%
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Average cross-validation results (combined models)",
    subtitle = "Mean R² and Deviance Explained across folds"
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(mean_R2, mean_DevianceExpl),
    decimals = 3
  )
```
